The editor’s notes
Thursday, 8 January, a video call between Bucharest and Madrid. Inés Vidal, the editor, has read Ecaterina’s manuscript. Marta joins in too, from Madrid.
Ecaterina, the book is wonderful, but I have to ask you to cut about forty pages.
Forty? And which ones would you recommend I cut?
I’d advise you to shorten the chapter about the trade office. Readers don’t need to know how a contract for tractors was translated.
Inés, that chapter made me laugh so much. Don’t let her take it out completely.
I can shorten it. But I beg you not to make me cut the night of 23 February.
Never. I forbid you to touch it. It’s the best thing in the book.
Then it’s a deal. Anything else?
Yes. The sales department insists that we change the title. They say “La lámpara encendida” sounds like an electricity manual.
How outrageous! My grandfather wouldn’t have let them say that.
Tell them to let me think about it for a week. And in the meantime, they’d better not dare change a single comma.

The “h” is silent, but the written accent shows that “í” is a separate syllable: pro-Í-bo (three syllables). In the infinitive the stress moves: pro-hi-BIR.
“g” before “i” sounds like the Spanish “j”: [ek-si-HIR]. In the first person it’s written with “j”: exijo [ek-SI-ho].
The diphthong “ue” is stressed: te-RUE-go. An “r” at the start of a word is rolled, like “rr”.
1. Verbs of influence + que + subjunctive
When someone tries to influence what SOMEONE ELSE does, “que” is followed by the subjunctive:
pedir, rogar, exigir, insistir en
Te pido que cortes cuarenta páginas.
aconsejar, recomendar, sugerir
Te aconsejo que acortes ese capítulo.
to forbid / to allow
prohibir, permitir, dejar
Te prohíbo que lo toques.
to oblige / to prevent
obligar a, impedir, hacer
Me obligó a que lo cortara.
If the subject is the same, use the infinitive, without “que”: «Quiero cortar» (I want, I cut), but «Quiero que cortes» (I want, you cut).
2. Infinitive or subjunctive?
With prohibir, permitir, dejar, obligar, aconsejar and recomendar you can ALSO use the infinitive, with an object pronoun:
They won’t let me go out.
He made me cut it.
I recommend you read it.
With “pedir”, “rogar”, “exigir” and “insistir en”, “que + subjunctive” is almost always used when the subjects are different.

Enero

In the first days of January, Ecaterina did nothing but wait. She got up at six, out of habit, switched on the computer, checked her email and switched it off again. She had sent many manuscripts in her life, but always translations: other people’s books, other people’s mistakes, other people’s successes. Now the book was hers, and the wait seemed as long as the one in 1987. Ana advised her to go out for a walk. Ecaterina replied that at her age you don’t go for a walk in Bucharest in January unless you want to freeze to death elegantly.

To keep from going mad, she began translating the first chapter into Romanian. It was a very strange feeling: for the first time in her life, the author she was translating was sitting in the same chair. When she couldn’t find a word, she couldn’t blame anyone. When a sentence sounded wrong in Romanian, she was tempted to change the original too. She told Ana that translating herself was like looking into a mirror that spoke another language, and the mirror argued with her as well.

Inés’s email arrived on 7 January, at eleven at night. It was long, affectionate and full of verbs Ecaterina knew very well from her years as a translator: I ask you, I recommend, I suggest, I forbid. She read it twice wearing Andrés’s tortoiseshell glasses, the ones Marta had given her at Christmas. They were a little too big and kept slipping down her nose, but she refused to take them off. She said that if she had to correct her book, she preferred him looking over her shoulder.

The next day they had a three-way video call: Inés from Barcelona, Marta from Madrid and Ecaterina from her living room, with Rosa Elena hidden under the table, because she had promised not to make a sound in exchange for being allowed to listen. Inés asked her to cut about forty pages. She advised her to shorten the chapter about the trade office, the one about the tractor contracts. Marta protested, because that chapter had made her laugh so much. Ecaterina agreed to shorten it, but begged Inés not to force her to touch the night of 23 February. Inés replied that she herself forbade it.

In Madrid, Andrei was living his last month as an intern. Begoña had commissioned a series of portraits of the city’s booksellers, and he spent his mornings going from bookshop to bookshop, with the film camera she had lent him again “so he wouldn’t forget how to wait”. Faustino had posed three times, each time in a different beret. The twins from Lavapiés had refused to pose together, and Andrei had had to take two identical portraits, one of each, to avoid a civil war.

The problem was the title. The publisher’s sales department insisted on changing it. According to them, “La lámpara encendida” sounded like an electricity manual, or a ghost story, or an advert for a lighting shop. They had proposed others: “The Bookseller of Madrid”, “Forty Years of Waiting”, “The Translator Who Came Back”. Marta said they were soap-opera titles. Ecaterina asked for a week to think about it and begged Inés, in the meantime, not to let anyone change a single comma.

When the club found out, the group chat filled up with suggestions. Costel suggested “The Lorry Driver Who Cried”, although Ecaterina reminded him that he wasn’t in the book. Mihai suggested “Always with Onion”. Mrs Florica, who had learnt to use her phone at Christmas, sent a two-minute voice message proposing “Soup for the Translator”, with very solid arguments. Señor Dan sent a table of the ten best-selling titles of the previous year and the average length of each in syllables. Nobody opened it.

When they hung up, Rosa Elena came out from under the table. She had listened to the whole conversation without moving, and she had a suggestion. She said the book had to be called “The Book Lorry”, because that was the nicest part. Ecaterina explained that there was no lorry in the book, because the story ended in 1987, long before Costel. Rosa Elena thought about it and told her to put it in the next book, then. Ecaterina promised that if she ever wrote another one, the lorry would be on the first page.

Over the following week, Ecaterina cut. Cutting hurt more than writing. The trade-office chapter, which had been thirty pages long, was reduced to six. She removed the director who took his siesta on top of the contracts, the Bulgarian driver who could only say “tractor” in five languages and the afternoon she mistakenly translated a love letter as if it were an order for spare parts. The only thing she refused to cut was one sentence of the director’s: “Miss Ionescu, I forbid you to fall in love during office hours.”

Inés had also suggested she shorten the chapter about her mother: the heart attack, the phone call at dawn, the plane to Bucharest the next day. She found it too harsh. Ecaterina wrote her a single sentence: “Please don’t ask me that: without that chapter, the rest of the book is the story of a woman who left for no reason.” Inés took ten minutes to reply. When she did, she wrote: “You’re right. Forgive me. Leave it exactly as it is.” Ecaterina didn’t change a word.

Meanwhile, in Bucharest, Costel and Señor Dan were waiting for their DELE results. Señor Dan checked the Instituto Cervantes website four times a day. Costel, who didn’t trust websites, called Ana every morning to ask whether she knew anything. In the end, Ana had to forbid it. She told them she would let them check the website once a week, on Mondays, and that if she caught them checking on any other day, she wouldn’t help them with the C1. They both obeyed. More or less.

The two of them had made bets. Señor Dan, with his table of practice tests, had calculated he would get 78 out of 100, with a margin of error of three points. Costel said a “pass” would do, even by one point, and the rest was vanity. Mrs Florica bet a pot of sarmale that they would both pass, and Ana refused to bet anything, because she thought it unprofessional. But in her notebook, on the last page, she had pencilled two marks, and she didn’t show them to anyone.

On 15 January, Rosa Elena turned six. They celebrated at home, with twelve children from kindergarten, three grandmothers, two cakes and a noise that, according to Señor Dan, exceeded all European noise-pollution standards. Rosa Elena had decided that this birthday would be in Spanish, and she made all the guests speak Spanish for a whole hour. The children from kindergarten didn’t know a word, so they spent the hour shouting “¡hola!” and “¡olé!”, which were the only things they had learnt from her.

In the middle of the afternoon the videos from Madrid arrived. Lola had filmed the lamp in the window switched on, with a handwritten sign underneath: “Happy birthday, Rosa Elena.” Faustino had filmed another from his stall, in his red beret, singing “Happy Birthday” so badly that the dogs on the Cuesta de Moyano started barking. And Andrei and Marta had filmed one together, in the hallway on the calle del Prado, in front of the green sign, with Rosa Elena’s drawing hanging beside it. Rosa Elena watched the three videos eleven times.

In the evening Grandpa Gheorghe called from the village. He didn’t know how to use video calls, so he rang the landline, and Ana put him on speaker. He sang Rosa Elena an old song nobody else knew, in the trembling voice of a ninety-six-year-old. Then he said to her, in the Spanish he had learnt in August, the only two words he remembered: “Por fin” and “salud”. Rosa Elena answered “olé”. Grandpa laughed so hard he had to hang up to cough.

Ecaterina gave her a children’s Spanish dictionary, with pictures, and wrote on the first page: “So you can help me write the lorry book.” Costel gave her a real lorry driver’s helmet, red, that was far too big for her. Ana forbade her to wear it at the table, so Rosa Elena wore it under the table. When she blew out the candles, nobody asked her to make her wish silently, because they knew by now it would be no use. She wished, out loud, that Ecaterina’s book would have a beautiful title.

The title wasn’t the only battle. The publisher also wanted to decide on the cover. The designer had proposed a photo bought from an image bank: an old lamp, very pretty and very fake, on a table that had never existed. Marta then remembered the photo she had taken in August, in Bucharest: the empty drawer of Ecaterina’s desk, where the letter had waited almost forty years. But she had taken that photo with her phone, at night, and it was blurred. A real one was needed.

Luckily, Andrei had taken one. On 30 December, the day before he went back to Madrid, Marta had asked him to photograph the drawer just in case, and he had spent a whole afternoon in Ecaterina’s bedroom, waiting for the light from the window to fall at exactly the right angle. He had taken a single photo, as Begoña had taught him. It showed the drawer open, empty, the wood worn, and at the bottom, almost invisible, the rectangular mark an envelope had left over forty years.

The designer said it was a beautiful photo, but too sad for a cover. The sales department said a drawer didn’t sell books. Andrei told Begoña, without asking her for anything. Begoña looked at the photo for a long time. Then she picked up the phone and dialled a number written in a paper diary from 1998. It turned out the publisher’s art director had worked with her on a newspaper twenty years earlier. The conversation lasted four minutes. Nobody ever found out what she said.

What nobody knew yet was what would happen to Andrei in February, when the internship ended. Begoña hadn’t mentioned the subject since October. Lucas was more nervous than Andrei himself: he advised him to ask her directly, not to wait, because in Madrid if you don’t ask, you don’t get. Andrei replied that Begoña had taught him to wait, and he wasn’t going to unlearn it now of all times. Lucas told him that was very poetic, but the rent wasn’t paid with poetry.

The next day, Inés called Ecaterina, delighted. The art director had insisted that the cover be the photo of the drawer, and had forbidden the use of any image-bank picture for that book. He had also demanded that the photographer’s name appear on the flap, in clearly visible letters. Andrei heard about it from Lucas, who shouted the news from the other end of the agency. Begoña, at her desk, didn’t look up from her screen. She only said: “Don’t thank me. It’s a good photo. Full stop.”

That left the title. Ecaterina spent the week turning it over in her mind, and the more she turned it over, the surer she was that she didn’t want to change it. On Friday evening she gathered the club in her living room and asked them to vote. She read them the publisher’s titles in a newsreader’s voice, and everyone laughed. Then she read her own. Costel voted for “La lámpara encendida” before she had finished reading it. Señor Dan voted the same, after making a table of pros and cons. Rosa Elena voted for “The Book Lorry”, on principle.

When everyone had gone, Ecaterina sat alone in the living room and remembered where the title came from. In the eighties, Andrés had a habit: every evening, at seven o’clock sharp, he switched on the lamp at the back of the bookshop, even if it was still light outside. She once asked him why. He told her it was so that people walking along calle de las Huertas would know he was still open. That a bookshop with its light on was an invitation. Ecaterina had never told anyone.

That same night, Ecaterina wrote a formal letter to the sales department. She used everything she had learnt in forty years of official letters: “Dear Sirs: I am writing to request that you allow me to keep the original title of the work.” She explained that the title wasn’t about electricity, but about a promise. That a lamp left on was what a man had left so that someone would come back. And she finished: “If, even so, you consider it necessary to change it, I would ask you to tell me in person, preferably in front of a bronze plaque on calle de las Huertas.”

The reply came three days later. The sales department accepted the title, on one condition: that it have a subtitle, so readers would know what the book was about. Ecaterina thought about it for a whole afternoon. In the end she proposed a very simple one: “Madrid, 1977 – Bucharest, 1987”. Inés replied with a single message: “Approved. And they’d better not dare ask you for anything else.” Marta, from Madrid, sent a photo of the plaque on calle de las Huertas, like a signature.

Pilar was the first to know, after Marta. She wrote to Ecaterina from Seville that she thought the subtitle was perfect, because those were exactly the ten years in which her father had been happiest, and also the ten years in which she had been a jealous little girl. Lola, for her part, printed the cover on a sheet of paper, with the title and subtitle, and stuck it in the window of El Mostrador, below the second lamp, with a sign: “Coming soon”. Customers began asking when it was coming out.

On 31 January, the postman handed Ecaterina a thick parcel from Barcelona. It was the proofs: the whole book, already typeset, with the pages exactly as they would be printed. Inés asked her to check them within two weeks and not to change anything important, only typos. Ecaterina sat down in her armchair, put on Andrés’s tortoiseshell glasses and opened the parcel. On the first page, on its own, in small print, was the dedication. She read it quietly. Then she turned the page, picked up her red pencil and began looking for typos, as she had done all her life with other people’s books.

At the end of page 212, Ecaterina stopped. There was the sentence Marta had given her on Christmas Eve: “She left because they needed her more than I did.” They had printed it in italics, without her asking. She looked in the margin for a note from Inés explaining it, but there was none. Later, Inés would confess it had been her decision: she had wanted that sentence to stand out from the rest, because it wasn’t Ecaterina’s or the novel’s, but belonged to someone who was no longer there. Ecaterina didn’t correct it.

That night she called Marta to read her page 212 over the phone. She told her the sentence was in italics and asked if it had been her idea. Marta swore it hadn’t. Then she was quiet for a moment and said that if anyone at the publisher tried to remove the italics, Ecaterina had permission to do whatever it took, even call Begoña. They both laughed. Before hanging up, Marta asked her to keep the first corrected proof for her, the one with the red pencil. Ecaterina promised to give it to her at the Madrid launch.
